Welcome To Week 1 of your Base Training Plan

The hardest part of this base plan is probably going to be learning to run slowly! Are you up for the challenge?

The purpose of base training is to improve your aerobic efficiency, so it is important you understand what “aerobic” means and why we are focussing on it.

Aerobic Vs Anaerobic

Nearly everybody will have heard the terms “aerobic” and “anaerobic” used in the context of running training, but not everybody understands what they mean.

Aerobic Training

Aerobic training essentially means that you are running/training at a low heart rate. It can also be thought of as running at an intensity which would allow you to carry out a conversation. During aerobic running you burn fat as your main source of energy. Aerobic training doesn’t put as much stress on your body as anaerobic training and you don’t need as much recovery time between training sessions, therefore you are less likely to suffer from injury or illness if the bulk of your training is aerobic.

Your aerobic system provides a solid foundation for good health. It is the system that builds up the muscles which help you to move efficiently throughout the day and support your overall posture. Training your aerobic system increases mitochondria in your muscle cells. These mitochondria generate energy (ATP) and improve your blood circulation which improves your body’s ability to utilise oxygen.

Aerobic conditioning is a necessary foundation of virtually all training. The longer an event, the more your body will rely on the aerobic system. A strong aerobic base will even benefit your recovery in-between sets of strength training as well as anaerobic interval training too.

Anaerobic Training

Anaerobic training is training at a higher heart rate, or an intensity at which you might only be able to speak two or three words before needing to draw another breath. It essentially means training without oxygen.

Anaerobic training puts a lot more stress on your body. It puts more stress on your muscles and joints because you are running at a faster pace. Anaerobic training sessions, like hill repeats or 1km intervals, take longer for your body to recover from, therefore, your training program needs to be structured to allow enough recovery time after these sessions to minimise the risk of you getting injured or sick.

How do you work out your Aerobic Heart Rate?

My first recommendation is to get a heart rate monitor (HRM) if you don’t already have one. In theory you could keep track of your heart rate by stopping at regular intervals throughout some runs to take your pulse manually, but a HRM will make it a lot easier to track accurately, and once you understand training with heart rate it can be an amazingly useful tool. Most watches now come with optical heart rate sensors, but in my experience most people will need either a chest strap or an arm band reader in order to get accurate measurements. The heart rate readings directly from a watch are much less reliable.

The key to using heart rate as a successful training tool is to work out your individual zones.

The most accurate way to do this is to get a lactate threshold test performed by a sports scientist. If you are not yet ready for that level of commitment, there are a number of formulas you can use which will approximate your training zones. In my opinion, the most accurate of these formulas is the 180 Formula which was devised by Phil Maffetone.

The 180 Formula

To find your maximum aerobic training heart rate there are two important steps.

- Subtract your age from 180

- Modify this number by selecting among the following categories the one that best matches your fitness and health profile.

(a) If you have, or are recovering from, a major illness (heart disease, any operation or hospital stay etc) or are on any regular medication, subtract and additional 10

(b) If you are injured, have regressed in training or competition, get more than two colds or bouts of flu per year, have allergies or asthma, or if you have been inconsistent or are just getting back into training, subtract an additional 5

(c) If you have been training consistently (at least 4 times/week) for up to two years without any of the problems in (a) and (b), keep the number (180-age) the same

(d) If you have been training for more than two years without any of the problems in (a) and (b), and have made progress in competition without injury, add 5.

For example, if you are 30 years old and fit into category (b), you get the following: 180-30 = 150. Then 150 – 5 = 145 beats per minute (bpm)

This number you have calculated is your Maximum Aerobic Heart Rate . Memorise it. This is the number we are going to use to govern the intensity at which you train.

Stop now and work out your aerobic threshold. Now you can make sure your “easy” training runs stay in the aerobic zone.

If your aerobic system is not very well developed you might find initially that running aerobically is frustratingly slow.

It takes 3 – 4 months of consistent aerobic training to start improving your aerobic system and gaining the benefits. Over these 3 -4 months you will gradually be able to run faster at any given heart rate, which is a sign that your aerobic system is improving.

If you have the discipline to train aerobically during your base training phase while everyone else is still hammering away with their normal hard training regime, it will pay huge dividends down the road.

How to Use the Plan

To use the 12 week base program properly, and to get the most benefit from it, you need to understand what all the session descriptions mean, so that you can use them to best effect in your training. You will see a number of shorthand descriptions which describe the particulars for that specific run. For example “ELEV” or “Flat” or “Rolling Hills”

To learn what these descriptions mean, please go to the Glossary tab.

Welcome To Week 2 of your Base Training Plan

I hope you enjoyed your first week on the 12 Week Base and Strength training plan.

The first week included an overview into how to identify your maximum aerobic heart rate threshold using the 180 Formula which was devised by Phil Maffetone. If you haven’t yet worked this out make sure you read the info tab on Week 1 of the plan. We will be using this to manage the intensity with which you train throughout the entire base training program.

This week we are going to spend some time working out your current level of:

- aerobic fitness

- running stability

Once you understand these two metrics, you wil be able to benchmark your performance throughout the program, and identify areas you need to work on.

How to Work out Your Current Aerobic Fitness

Perform a Maximum Aerobic Function (MAF) test.

Once you have calculated your Maximum Aerobic Training Heart Rate (MATHR) using the 180 Formula, you should perform a MAF test. This will give you an objective measure of your current level of aerobic fitness, which we can then retest at various intervals throughout the training plan as a way of gauging your progress.

How do you perform a MAF Test?

- You need to perform this test on flat ground. You can use an athletics track, a sports oval, or any stretch of uninterrupted (no traffic lights or pedestrian crossings) pavement or road.

- Take note of the ambient temperature and humidity level.

- Warm up slowly for 15 minutes.

- The actual test is a 5km flat run, sticking as close as possible to your MATHR number. Record the exact time splits for each kilometre.

- Cool down for 10 minutes.

Example: Mark’s Test: My MATHR is 144bpm.

- Warm up for 15 minutes making sure that your heart rate is up around the MATHR number towards the end of the warm up.

- Now go straight into the test without stopping or cooling down.

- Start your watch and try to keep your heart rate as close to MATHR (144 for me) as possible, for the entire duration of the 5km test. Continue running for the 5km without stopping.

- Cool down for 10 minutes, finishing with a walk for the last 2 – 3 minutes.

- Look back at your watch data and get the time splits for each 1km interval during the test. 1 st Kilometre – 5:00 2 nd Kilometre – 5:01 3 rd Kilometre – 5:05 4 th Kilometre – 5:30 5 th Kilometre – 6:00

- 1 st Kilometre – 5:00

- 2 nd Kilometre – 5:01

- 3 rd Kilometre – 5:05

- 4 th Kilometre – 5:30

- 5 th Kilometre – 6:00

- Record these times. They are the numbers we need to retest in 4 weeks, 8 weeks and monthly from then on.

- If your splits do not get progressively slower, it usually means that you did not warm up enough, so repeat the test on another day with a better warm up.

Using my example, you can see that towards the back end of the test my pace drops away. This means that I have to slow down quite early in a run to make sure I remain within my aerobic training zone which means I am not very aerobically efficient.

If I was to maintain my 5:00/k pace (rather than sticking to the 144 HR), then my heart rate would have climbed above 144bpm, which means I would be training anaerobically and putting my joints, muscles and immune system under more stress.

If you train consistently within your aerobic heart rate zone for a period of 2- 3 months, then you should see a significant improvement in your aerobic efficiency.

What this would mean for me, is that by the end of this 12 week base training plan, I would hope to see my 1km splits change to something like:

- 1 st Kilometre – 4:40

- 2 nd Kilometre – 4:45

- 3 rd Kilometre – 4:55

- 4 th Kilometre – 5:05

- 5 th Kilometre – 5:25

This means it now requires less effort for me to run at 5mins/km, so I can maintain that pace for longer. OR I can now run faster for a given level of effort. Either way, I have become a faster, more efficient runner, and I have improved my endurance ability.

Please note that it might take longer than 12 weeks to see a significant change with your MAF tests. The longer you continue with an aerobic training plan the more efficient you will become.

How strictly do you have to stick to the MATHR in training?

According to Dr Maffetone, you should never go over this MATHR number. This means a lot of you will be needing to walk up most, if not every, hill when you are training. You might even have to walk on the flats on a hot day if your aerobic system doesn’t work well.

Personally, I think there is a little bit of “room for error” and it is more realistic to aim to keep your average HR for a run below the MATHR number.

Using my 144HR example. During a 10km hilly trail run my HR might be 135bpm on the flats, but might climb to 160bpm on the hills if I was to run continuously. To keep my HR in the correct zone on average, I would, in this case, run up a hill until my HR reached 150bpm, then start walking, and when my HR was back down to 135 – 138bpm I would start running again. This way I should manage to keep my average HR for the entire run at just under 144.

Does all of your training have to be aerobic?

The purpose of the base training phase is to develop your aerobic system to make you stronger and more efficient, so that the transition to the harder, race-specific training block is an easy one.

For this reason, almost all of the Base Training Phase will be aerobic, and during this 12 week period I would hope that you can feel enough benefits that you want to stick to it. It can be an amazing eye opener for some runners to realise how much better their body feels, how much quicker they recover from training, and how much more consistently they can run, when they train aerobically.

There will be some accelerations included in the training plan which will help to add some training variety and also help you to maintain some leg speed.

Why do you need to record the temperature and humidity?

In order for the MAF test to be accurate, you should ideally perform it under the same conditions. This includes the climatic conditions. Depending on the time of the year this can be very difficult, especially as you head into summer.

Warmer weather and increased humidity will elevate your heart rate, so if changes in weather conditions are unavoidable between tests, then you need to factor this into your results.

Should you perform the MAF test if you have a cold or flu or other illness?

No. Wait until you feel well again. When you are ill your heart rate is generally elevated which will have a significant effect on the results.

This topic always raises a lot of questions.

Here is a list of frequently asked questions and answers to help you understand how to incorporate aerobic training into your weekly program.

What are the negative impacts of doing a little bit of anaerobic training each week in base training? (e.g. a hiit class, hill reps or a hard run)

The major benefit of training your aerobic system is to develop more endurance, become more efficient at burning fat (which can be a major benefit in endurance events), developing stronger muscles, tendons and bones, all whilst staying healthy and strong. Aerobic training does not create the same levels of impact and fatigue as anaerobic training which makes it easier to build up your running volume with less risk of injuries occurring.

Every time you do an anaerobic training session you interfere with your body’s aerobic adaptation process, and therefore you reduce your fat burning, compromise your immune system, create more fatigue, and put your body at slightly more risk of injury.

Once you have built a strong aerobic base, your body will become robust enough to withstand and benefit from the short blocks of anaerobic training which occur in the lead up to the race.

You will not develop your aerobic system to its full potential if you consistently perform anaerobic sessions.

Can I do any other races during this base training block?

You can. But you will be compromising your aerobic development. If you have other races booked in I would strongly suggest that you treat them like a “fun run”. If you are completely disciplined and dedicated to your aerobic development then stick to your MATHR during the race. If you can’t resist the temptation (which realistically most of you probably can’t) then try to run at around an 80% effort, with enough left in the tank to be able to go for a 10km “cool down” straight after the race if someone asked you to.

(For the purpose of clarity: Don’t actually do the 10km cool down, just be capable of doing it post race).

Can I do my regular pilates / yoga / stretching classes instead of the body maintenance each week?

I would suggest replacing only one of the sessions with your class each week. The exercises in the base program are very run-specific so you will get a huge amount of benefit out of doing them consistently and regularly. It all comes down to your main priority. If your main priority is your class, then of course you can choose to do that, but it may compromise your race result or your ability to get through all of the running training injury-free.

Should I work on my cadence whilst focussing on my aerobic heart rate?

One repercussion of increasing your cadence is that it also increases your heart rate. So if you are new to either aerobic training and/or running technique it can be a very difficult combination. My suggestion would be to spend the first 2 – 3 weeks sticking strictly to the MATHR, then very gradually start increasing your cadence by a few steps at a time. e.g. from 165 steps/minute up to 168 steps/minute. Give yourself some time to adapt to the higher cadence and then aim for a further increase as your MATHR allows.

How important is the warm up when we do the MAF test? What difference does it make?

At the end of the warm up your heart rate should be at your MATHR level – otherwise your first couple of km’s of the MAF test become your warm up which has a significant effect on the results. It is very important to warm up properly.

What other factors influence my heart rate when I train?

The biggest factors which will effect your heart rate, and therefore your ability to train aerobically are:

- External stresses (work stress for example)

- Lack of sleep

- Poor diet

- Alcohol

- Caffeine

- Illness (colds and flus)

If you are having a really busy week at work and it is causing excessive stress, it will elevate your heart rate. During these stressful weeks, don’t perform a MAF test. Do it once life is back under control.

Accept the simple fact that not everything is going to be under your full control all of the time. A bad night’s sleep, or a poor diet for a day or two will affect your heart rate, so you might have to train slower as a result. This doesn’t mean you are losing fitness . It just means that external factors are effecting your body.

I don’t honestly know how I can stick to the plan if I am having to walk on most runs to stay under my MEF heart rate

That is a choice only you can make. In my opinion, if you have to walk to stay under your MATHR, then you are one of the people who will gain the most benefit from doing it. You will not lose fitness, and you will not compromise your race preparation in the slightest, by training slowly during this 12 week plan.

At the very least try to stick with the aerobic training for 5 weeks until we do the second MAF test. At that point if you feel like your brain can’t cope (your brain is the issue because your body will be loving it) then you can speed up again and give the heart rate training a miss.

Could my heart rate monitor be the problem?

Unfortunately this is possible. In my experience chest straps and arm bands give by far the most reliable readings. The wrist optical sensors are fairly well recognised for not giving accurate readings. There may be runs where the heart rate numbers seem to jump around quite a lot, or suddenly change from say 180bpm to 130bpm – this is likely a glitch with the technology, but if it happens regularly it would be worth consulting with your GP to organise an exercise stress test and make sure it isn’t your internal hardware that is at fault!

Can I use perceived effort instead of heart rate?

You can if you really feel like heart rate training is not for you. The main problem with perceived effort is that if you have always run “too fast” then you don’t actually know what “easy” means.

One thing you could try to test your perceived effort accuracy is to sing a song out loud while you run. Seriously. Loud enough for people to hear. If you are singing 6 – 8 words at a time between breaths then you will be somewhere close to your aerobic zone. Don’t cheat though. Singing in your head or under your breath is not the same as singing out loud! You could also try a run whilst breathing only through your nose (no mouth breathing at all) – if you can nose breathe then you should also be in your aerobic zone.

If you have the discipline to train aerobically during your base training phase, when everyone else is still hammering away, it will pay you dividends down the road.

Stability Vs Strength – How Stable Are you?

For the first few weeks of the plan, your strength and stability workout will have more of an emphasis on stability.

If you have a stable “core” when you run you are much less likely to get injured. This will allow you to train consistently, and training consistently, especially on hills, will make you stronger.

If you have followed any of my programs previously, you will already (or should have) tested your stability. Give it a go now and write down your results.

Test your stability now

To get an understanding of stability, I want you to do this simple one minute test. Stand on one leg, close your eyes. Start counting in seconds 1, 2, 3…………

How long did you last until you had to put your foot down?.

If you made it to

- less than 10… You have a lot of work to do

- 10 – 30 ……. Still not good. Your lack of hip stability might cause some injuries

- 30 – 45 …….. Better, but still room for improvement

- 60 seconds …….. Great. Keep doing what you are doing

Write down your score for both legs. We will revisit this later in the program and see how you have improved.

notes.text: This week we are introducing stair hiking to the program. THESE ARE WALKING REPEATS – NOT RUNNING. Find a set of stairs with around 50 – 100 steps if possible. You should perform these stair repeats during the middle portion of your run (after a short warm up and before a short cool down). For these stair repeats you should initially walk up 1 step at a time, but you can progress to 2 steps at a time if you can keep your heart rate low (this depends on your level of aerobic fitness). Walk slowly back down the stairs to recover. Repeat for the stated duration on the training plan.

notes.label: Technique
notes.text:
I would normally introduce some running technique lessons in week one of a training program, however, given this is a base training program, I wanted to make sure you first understood:

- the concept of aerobic training, and your own training zones (week 1)

- how to calculate your Maximum aerobic heart rate and Performing a Maximum Aerobic Function (MAF) test (week 2)

I know, that for most of you this will have been a struggle. Running slow can be frustrating. However, it really works. So please try and stick with it.

Now we are going to cover some running technique

Below you will see some information on how to improve your cadence. For now, running to your maximum aerobic heart rate is your priority . I find that shortening your stride and concentrating on your running form can help give you something to focus on when your mind starts to complain about the slow pace. So focus on your technique during your base training and you will reap the rewards when you step up to the harder training sessions in a race training plan.

You need to start by working on the absolute foundation of what will lead to a successful trail race. Your running technique. It doesn’t matter how many stretches or exercises you do, if your running technique is not up to scratch, you will be much more likely to suffer a number of common running injuries and you will never reach your full potential.

This video will show you exactly what to focus on to improve your technique. There is also a video which shows you what to focus on to improve your speed. Don’t put the cart before the horse though. Perfect your general running technique before worrying about running fast. (particularly whilst in your base training phase)

The three most important components of running technique are:

- Posture – stand up tall

- Cadence – 175 – 185 steps/minute

- Short Strides – foot landing close to under your body

In the running technique video I refer to the importance of running with the correct cadence. Cadence is the number of steps per minute you take. There is a bit of controversy around whether there is a specific number you should aim for.

I am a huge believer that 180 is the gold standard and something that you should all ultimately be aiming for.

What should you do to improve your cadence?

The best way to work on improving your cadence is to use a metronome. You can buy a small, clip-on, digital metronome that is perfect for the purpose, or if you run with your phone, you can download a metronome app and use that. Set the metronome to the appropriate beat, and run in time with the beeps (one foot landing each time you hear a beep).

FOLLOW THESE STEPS TO MAKE SURE YOU DO IT ACCURATELY AND SAFELY

- Measure your cadence. During the middle of a normal training run, count your steps for a minute on a section of flat ground. Repeat this several times over several runs to work out an accurate average.

- It is difficult to increase your cadence by more than 10steps/minute in any one go. If your cadence is 160, for example, you should set your metronome to 170 and get used to that for a month, before increasing it further to 180.

- Continue using the metronome for as long as you need to until 180 becomes your natural / subconscious gait pattern

If you like running with music, it is possible to use an App to play music at a certain number of beats per minute. It is much harder though, to follow the rhythm of music than it is to follow the simple beat of a metronome, so I would highly recommend using a simple metronome App initially, and once you have become accustomed to the higher cadence and it feels natural, then you could switch back to running with music.

As I already mentioned, it can be difficult to work on too many things at once.

Priority 1 – stick to your maximum aerobic heart rate

Priority 2 – start thinking about your cadence

We will revisit your cadence towards the end of the program. So don’t worry if you can’t get both of these right just yet.

Congratulations – You have made it to week 4

Your Base Training So Far

- Week 1 – You worked out your aerobic heart rate and we introduced the first 4 weeks of strength and stability

- Week 2 – You learn’t how to calculate your maximum aerobic heart rate and perform a Maximum Aerobic Function (MAF) test. We also did a stability test to see how stable you are.

- Week 3 – We started to look at your cadence and ways to improve it.

To get the most from the program, I really encourage you to do all the tests and activities I recommend each week. We will do some of these again in the coming weeks, so it is important you have a baseline to track your improvements and identify areas to focus on.

Your butt / glute muscles are so important in running that I am going to dedicate a whole section to it!

The Gluteus Maximus muscle is the biggest muscle in your body. If it doesn’t function properly (and subconsciously) when you run, then you are going to be using other muscles to compensate. Not using glute max efficiently can result in knee pain, hip flexor pain, lower back pain and more.

By functioning subconsciously, I mean it should just work. You shouldn’t have to be concentrating on “keeping it switched on”. If you do that when you run then you will probably lose focus on other, more important aspects of good running form.

Teaching your brain how to activate Glute Max is vital before you attempt to strengthen it.

So how do you work out if you have a lazy bum?

Most people spend so much of their life in a seated position (breakfast – car – work – lunch – work – car – dinner – sofa) that they develop a “lazy bum”. What I mean by a “lazy bum” is that the nerve connection between your brain and your bum gets disrupted. It is a bit like having faulty wiring in your house. Think of your brain as the light switch and your bum as the light bulb. If the wiring is faulty the light bulb doesn’t work properly. If your “wiring” (nerve pathways) are faulty from years of sitting, then your glute muscles don’t work properly.

Take the test: Watch this video which explains how to switch on your gluteus maximus and find out if you can do it.

Did you pass the test?

If you found it easy to activate your gluteus maximus, and you could easily switch it on and off without all the surrounding muscles trying to help out, then you can safely work on strengthening your glutes.

Did you fail the test?

Did you stand there trying to squeeze your bum tight and nothing happened? or did your quads tightened instead? If this was the case then you need to practice switching on your glutes every day.

Really, you shouldn’t be working on glute strengthening exercises like lunges and squats because instead of building up your glutes, you will actually be strengthening the muscles which are already working too hard like your quads and your hip flexors. If you do have hip flexor or knee issues then make sure you practice switching your glutes on before you start any of the strength routines, and if your pain persists then see your local running physio to get some more 1-on-1 help.

As frustrating as it is, you need to practice and practice and practice until you can “switch on your glutes” – Don’t give up trying.

One day they will work . Practice this glute activation a few times every day. The more you try, the faster your brain will make the connection.

It only takes 30 seconds, and you can do it almost anywhere.

This week I want you to spend 15-20 seconds switching on each glute before you run and before any strength and stability training sessions to improve the chances of them working efficiently.

Recovery Week

Good news. This week is a recovery week, so the long run is slightly shorter and the Friday session is slightly easier if you are on the beginner or intermediate plans. Because this is a base training plan, and the volume and intensity is still quite low, the reduction in training this week is only a small one.

Despite the reduced running volume, this is NOT A REST WEEK . You need to continue with the same number of runs per week and be just as diligent (if not, more so) with your body maintenance sessions. A week of complete rest will probably leave you feeling tired and sluggish and less motivated to get back into the training next week. The aim of the recovery week is to keep your body and your brain used to running, whilst still logging some all-important km’s in the training diary.

This week we are introducing our new series of strength and stability activities.

These are 2o minute Running-Specific Strength Workouts designed to help improve your balance and stability, as well as strengthening the muscle groups which help you run: glutes, quads, hamstrings and calf muscles.

Equipment: Ideally to perform these full workouts you will need a light kettlebell and a skipping rope. However, a 2 litre bottle of water can be used as a kettlebell substitute, and you can jump on the spot without a skipping rope if you don’t have these items.

If you are new to kettlebell training, and you don’t have a lot of upper body strength, then you should start with a 2kg kettlebell. If you are used to kettlebell training, lifting weights, or you generally have good upper body strength then you should start with a 4kg kettlebell. Over time you can progress up to 6kg and ultimately 8kg as your strength improves. It is important to use an appropriate weight that allows you to maintain good technique.

notes.text:
This Week’s Focus: Nutrition for Enhanced Training

Proper nutrition is as vital as training and recovery in achieving your goals. Let’s explore how to ensure your diet supports rather than hinders your progress.

Prioritise Real Food

Adopting the “JERF” (Just Eat Real Food) principle is a simple yet effective approach to meal and snack choices. Also known as a “whole foods” diet, this means prioritising foods that are minimally processed or unprocessed—those that come directly from the ground, trees, or animals.

Such a nutrient-dense diet promotes overall health and well-being, not only by providing essential nutrients but also by avoiding harmful additives like refined sugars, chemicals, preservatives, and highly refined vegetable oils. These substances can disrupt your metabolism, hormones, and liver function.

Remember, the food you eat supplies the body with the nutrients it needs for cell growth, DNA replication, and tissue repair—directly impacting your muscles, ligaments, immune system, and vitality. In essence: you are what you eat.

How to Improve Nutrition: Meal Planning

The most impactful change you can make is planning your meals in advance. Keeping healthy, prepared food readily available in your fridge sets you up for success.

Establishing good habits now will be invaluable as your weekly mileage increases and your energy needs grow. With more time dedicated to training, efficiency and organisation in meal prep become critical.

Weight Management and Macronutrients

During the base training phase, meeting your energy needs is crucial to support muscle growth, bolster your immune system, and prevent injuries. This involves finding the right balance of carbohydrates, protein, and healthy fats to match your goals and training load.

Protein Requirements: Athletes generally need 1.2–1.5g of protein per kilogram of body weight . For example, a 70kg athlete should consume 85–105g of protein daily.

Here’s a rough guide to protein content:

- Meat, poultry, fish: ~25–30g per 100g (cooked)

- Eggs: ~8g per large egg

- Legumes, seeds, nuts, whole grains, dark green veggies: Also great protein sources

Key Tip: Spread protein intake throughout the day. Since the body can only absorb about 40g of protein at one time, aim for 20–30g per meal , supplementing with snacks.

Recovery Nutrition: The Most Important Meal

Your post-training meal is essential for replenishing muscle glycogen, supporting protein synthesis, and reducing cortisol levels (to avoid adrenal fatigue).

Consume this meal within 45 minutes of training and ensure it includes a balance of protein, carbohydrates, and healthy fats.

Post-Training Meal Ideas:

- Breakfast: Fruit with yogurt, nuts, seeds, or muesli Eggs with toast, spinach, or avocado Smoothie Frittata with potato/sweet potato or corn Porridge made with milk, topped with fruit and seeds

- Fruit with yogurt, nuts, seeds, or muesli

- Eggs with toast, spinach, or avocado

- Smoothie

- Frittata with potato/sweet potato or corn

- Porridge made with milk, topped with fruit and seeds

- Dinner: Chicken stir-fry with brown rice Steak with sweet potato and greens Grilled fish with buckwheat, beetroot, and spinach salad Homemade burgers with a large leafy green salad

- Chicken stir-fry with brown rice

- Steak with sweet potato and greens

- Grilled fish with buckwheat, beetroot, and spinach salad

- Homemade burgers with a large leafy green salad

Hydration Tips

During exercise, you lose water through sweat and respiration—on average, about 800ml per hour (temperature-dependent). Since the body can only absorb 600–700ml per hour , it’s important to hydrate consistently throughout the day, sipping water rather than drinking large amounts all at once.

Additionally, sweat causes electrolyte loss, primarily sodium. As training intensifies, consider using electrolyte supplements (e.g., Nuun, Hydralyte) before or after long runs. Sodium helps the body retain hydration effectively.

If you’re a heavy sweater or often feel thirsty, aim to include 1–2 servings of electrolytes per week.

Summary

- Follow the “JERF” principle—eat minimally processed food from natural sources.

- Get organised with meal planning and preparation.

- Include protein with every meal, aiming for 20–30g per meal and smaller amounts in snacks.

- Consume a balanced recovery meal within 45 minutes post-training.

- Stay hydrated throughout the day and replenish electrolytes as needed.

By aligning your nutrition with your training, you’ll optimise performance, recovery, and overall well-being.

notes.text:
Stair Technique

Trail events are typically riddled with hills and stairs. Stairs can trash your legs if not handled properly.

If your technique is not efficient when negotiating stairs – both upstairs and downstairs – you will be creating unnecessary fatigue in your muscles, and stress on your joints.

Make the stairs something to look forward to by improving your technique and powering past people on race day.

Running Upstairs

- Stay upright so you use primarily your glute muscles

- Take the stairs one at a time. This is easier on your heart and lungs and your quads than trying to tackle them two at a time.

- Depending on the depth and height of the stairs, try to get your whole foot on the step when you can. This is also relevant walking up stairs. If your foot lands flat (as opposed to on your toes on the front edge of the step) then your calf muscles will get a rest.

Walking Upstairs

Walking upstairs is a lot more energy efficient than running up, in my experience you will definitely be walking up stairs at some point during a trail race, so it is worth getting in some practice.

In general, the same rules apply for walking upstairs as running upstairs. Try not to bend over. This tires your quads

If the stairs are very steep and it feels difficult to physically continue running, then you are better off walking and saving some energy. The amount of time you might lose walking up these steep sections is negligible compared to the amount of time you can lose later in the race if you have “blown up”

Watch this video on stair running technique to learn how to run efficiently both up and down stairs.

Running downstairs

Use every step. Don’t try and take them two at a time. If they are really steep there is often a handrail, so use the handrail to ease some of the load on your quads. Hiking poles can also be useful for this if you are worried about whether your quads or knees will survive the event.

If the stairs are very technical then you can use your arms as a type of counter balance. Keeping them high and wide can help to improve your stability as your body weight shifts from side to side.

In summary, the four most important components of stair running/walking are:

- Posture – stand up tall and use your glutes instead of relying on your quads.

- Take Every Step – quick small steps uses less energy

- Upstairs Walking – try not to bend over. It tires your quads

- Downstairs – Take every step. Flow down like water, taking the path of least resistance to reduce the impact on joints

Is your stability improving?

So far, you have spent a lot of time working on your stability (if you have completed all your workouts!)

If you have a stable “core” when you run you are much less likely to get injured.

In week 2 we tested your stability. I want you to do it again now

One Minute Stability Test

Stand on one leg, close your eyes. Start counting in seconds 1, 2, 3…………

How long did you last until you had to put your foot down?.

If you made it to

- less than 10… You have a lot of work to do

- 10 – 30 ……. Still not good. Your lack of hip stability might cause some injuries

- 30 – 45 …….. Better, but still room for improvement

- 60 seconds …….. Great. Keep doing what you are doing

Write down your score for both legs. Compare it to your week 2 results, and we will revisit it again later in the program and see how you have improved.

How To Improve Your Downhill Trail Running Technique

Last week, we covered your technique for running up and down stairs. This week, we are going to talk about running downhill.

If you can’t run downhills confidently, you’ll never reach your true racing potential.

One of the easiest and fastest ways to improve your downhill running is to improve your technique. Just like running on the flat, when you run downhill you should be taking small steps and keeping your cadence high.

When we run downhill gravity is doing a lot of the work for us, so it doesn’t put much stress on our heart and lungs. Because of this, it is easy to inadvertently overstride when you speed up.

If you keep your strides short and increase your cadence it will help to save your quads and knees from injury.

Watch this video to learn more about downhill running technique:

How many of you have ever practised downhill reps?

- Doing Downhill reps is so rare that is actually sounds a bit stupid. Why waste your time doing downhill reps when you could be making yourself stronger by running uphills?

The best way to gain more confidence running downhills is to practice running downhills.

I recommend you practice your downhill technique as part of your weekend long trail run.

Make sure you start with an easy session and add this mid way through your long weekend run.

An example of a downhill training session to start with:

- Find a hill of about 100m long at a gentle gradient of about 5-6 degrees. Warm up by running for 10-15 minutes, then do 5 hill repeats where you run up slowly, or walk up to keep your heart rate low, and run down at a “steady” effort. By “steady” I mean the sort of effort you would put in if you were trying to get a 10km PB. At the end of the reps you can continue with the rest of your easy long weekend trail run.

- Don’t worry about your pace on these downhill reps, just focus on the level of effort. Your pace might be faster than 10km race pace because you are doing them downhill.

- I will even let you go over your Maximum Aerobic Threshold for the downhill, but it will only be for about 15 – 20 secs per downhill rep, so your average heart rate will still stay low.

What should your cadence be when running down a hill?

I am a firm believer that we should all run with a cadence of between 175 – 185 steps/minute. I covered this earlier in the program (refer to Week 1 and 2).

A cadence of less than 175 puts more stress on your calf muscles and achilles tendons. A cadence of higher than 185 puts more stress on your heart and lungs, without there being any additional benefit in terms of reducing your stride length or improving your calf muscle efficiency.

When we run downhills and gravity is working with us, your heart and lungs don’t have to work very hard, so it is ok to let your cadence increase (even up to 200 – 210 steps/minute) if it helps to keep your stride short. It all comes down to how fast you want to be running.

If you are happy “cruising” down a hill at a comfortable pace, then a cadence of 180 and a short stride is perfect.

If you are racing down a hill at the edge of your comfort zone, then a cadence of 200 and a short stride, is preferable to a cadence of 180 and a long stride.

Week 8 of your Base Training

This week, I wanted to cover a question I am frequently asked about A and B races.

Often people have a major race during the year and they want to know if they can do smaller races prior to their ‘A’ race. So how do you work a B race into your training schedule?

What are the benefits of B races?

B races are a great way to gauge your current level of fitness, gain some valuable race practice and they will also help to maintain your training motivation. Most runners find it easier to train consistently if they are training for an event, rather than just running for the sake of staying fit. If your goal race is 9 months away, it can seem too far away to really “need” to train, and therefore the motivation levels can drop off.

B races are an excellent way to plan and practice what you intend to do on the day of the big race.

This might include:

- Eating the same breakfast.

- Doing the same stretching / warm up routine.

- Using the same gear / equipment.

- Testing your race day nutrition strategy

- Testing combinations of shoes, socks and clothes

If any of these things go wrong on the day of the big dance it can have a terrible effect on your overall performance. Training hard for 6 – 9 months, only to make a simple error on race day is both frustrating and de-motivating in terms of wanting to get back out there and race again. If you put in the hard yards training, then you deserve to get an awesome result at the end of it all.

B races are the perfect opportunity to make your mistakes, and correct them, so you minimise the chances of things going wrong during your goal race.

John Vs Jane Vs the UTA 50k Trail Run

It is probably easiest to explain the philosophy behind B Races using an example of two different runners with the same “A” race in their calendar.

Jane has entered the UTA50. She has been running consistently for 15 years with minimal injuries. She has run the UTA50 twice in the past, along with numerous other ultra events and she is looking to beat her time in the UTA this year. To do this she has to be able to maintain a steady/hard level of effort for the entire duration of the race.

John has also entered the UTA50. He has been running for 9 months and his mates talked him into entering the UTA over a few beers at the pub one night. He has already completed a half marathon, but pulled up with fairly sore knees, so needed a couple of weeks off running to recover. His aim for the UTA50 is to finish it without completely wrecking himself, and hopefully beat one or two of his drinking buddies in the process.

The UTA50 is in May, both Jane and John are looking for some “B” races in the lead up to the UTA.

What length event should you choose for your B race?

This is very dependent on your level of running experience and your history of injuries.

Jane chooses to do the Six Foot Track (45km, 1500m vert) 8 weeks out, and Mt Solitary Ultra (45km, 2500m vert) 4 weeks out from the UTA. She knows Mt Solitary is a hard race, but she has done it before and knows that if she runs it at 80% she can recover within a week and get back to her intended UTA training program.

Jane does Six Foot at 90% effort, and is training well again within a week, she also does Mt Solitary, but only at about 70% effort due to a few niggles and the fact that she is feeling more tired than usual. Again, she pulls up ok, and is quickly back on track for the last little spurt of UTA training. She smashes the UTA and gets a 15 minute PB.

John chooses to do the Six Foot Track (45km, 1500m vert) 8 weeks out, and The Jabulani Challenge (45km, 1500m vert) 4 weeks out from the UTA. He has never raced more than 21.1km before, but figures that a couple of 45km training events will get him in great nick for the UTA.

John does Six Foot at 90% effort. He finishes with very sore knees, and also now a painful foot. He needs 2 weeks completely off running, before he carefully eases back into some gentle training.

He wisely decides not to do the Jabulani Challenge, and he makes it to the start line of the UTA averaging only 20km of running per week for the final 8 weeks of his program. Needless to say, the UTA is not much fun, and John’s goal of beating his drinking buddies was over before he even made it to the start line.

What criteria should you use to choose your B race?

- Err on the side of caution. The maximum amount of time you can afford to recover from a B race is 7 – 10 days. Don’t enter a B race if you are not confident that you will pull up ok.

- Run at an intensity which allows you to pull up ok – You might need to treat it like a big training day, or a race practice day, rather than an actual race.

- Don’t fall into the trap of doing a B race purely for the psychological benefits (John would have felt confident going into the UTA having done a 45km race, but very nervous if he’d only done a 30km race – BUT, his UTA would have been much more successful had he only done a 30km lead up race)

- If you are relatively new to running (less than 3 consistent years) and/or your “A” goal is further than you have ever attempted, then again you should err on the side of caution and choose shorter/easier lead up races that you are confident that you can recover from quickly.

When should your B races be timed?

Once again, this will depend very much on the individual, and also on the length of your goal race.

An 800m track runner for example might race every weekend of the season, and be very successful with this strategy.

An experienced 100K runner might do a 45km race four weeks out, and a 20km race two weeks out to help “sharpen themselves up”.

As a general rule of thumb I would time your B Race to allow 1 week per 10km’s raced. So a 30km B Race, three weeks out from the goal would be ok, but a 50km race three weeks out would be too much.

If you are likely to be towards the mid-tail end of a field, then it might be better to use hours rather than km’s. Allow 1 week for every 1 hour raced. The reason for this is that it might take a fast runner 3 hours for their 30km B race, but it might take a slower runner 5 hours for the same 30km B race. You won’t fully recover from a 5 hour B race in three weeks.

The absolute bottom line behind having a successful goal race is consistent training. Your choice of “B” races can either make you, or break you. So please choose your B races carefully.

Do you use poles when trail running?

Even on a relatively runnable course poles could help you to run faster . They help to take some of the load that your legs would otherwise have to take. This means your legs will have more strength for later in the race to power your way to the finish line.

Trail running guru Scotty Hawker talks of his experience where he ran without poles in Laveredo Ultra-Trail in Italy, and how it probably cost him a place or two.

If you’re thinking about using poles in your next event then make sure you get plenty of practice with them in training. There is both technique and skill involved to get the most out of them. Watch this video and learn Scotty’s tips for how to handle poles and how to use them efficiently.

We are reaching the end of your 12 week program

During the program we have covered

- Aerobic v’s anaerobic training

- Running technique’s for all types of terrain

- Improved your strength and stability and hopefully developed a life long Body Maintenance Routine

- Worked on your cadence

As you head into a race training block, you will probably be wondering what you need to do to become a faster runner! There are two other factors that I believe are key;

1. CONSISTENCY IS KEY

Consistency is what allows you to keep progressing. The annual injury rate of recreational runners is up to 56%. If you can properly manage both your training load and your body, and string together months of uninterrupted and consistent training, you wont have to waste any time trying to get fit, because you’ll already be fit! You’ll be able to build on the gains you have already made, and continue to take your running from strength to strength.

To achieve this injury-free consistency you need to schedule “Body Maintenance” regimes into your weekly training schedule.

So stick with your body Maintenance!

Runners have a very bad habit, when lacking time, of still managing to do every run in their training diary, but skipping the body maintenance sessions. They feel they will get more benefit out of logging more k’s of training, than working on improving their strength and stability.

I highly recommend making your body maintenance work equal in importance to your running training.

Strength and stability training combined with regular stretching and rolling will keep your muscles and joints moving efficiently and will help you to maintain good form when you run. Running with good form during a race will help you to maintain a faster overall pace.

2. FOCUS ON YOUR FORM.

In the quest for more speed, focusing on your running form is one of the easiest ways to make big gains.

The keys to good form are:

- Posture – stand up tall, with a slight lean forward from the ankles (not the hips)

- Cadence – turn your legs over quickly (around 180 steps/minute)

- Short Strides – Your foot should land relatively close to under your body

So in your quest to get faster, focus on form and consistency are key. Not thrashing it out around the track once a week!

glossary.definition:
For your Base Training Plan you will see a number of shorthand descriptions which describe the details for that specific run. For example “ELEV” or “MAF Test”

To use this training plan properly, and to get the most benefit from it, you need to understand what these session descriptions mean, so that you can use them to best effect in your training.

Choose your training level – Beginner, Intermediate or Advanced?

🔰 Beginner Plan This plan is ideal if you’re new to structured training or coming back from a break. You should be comfortable running or run/walking around 15–20km per week across 3–4 sessions, with a long run of about 6km. Over 12 weeks you’ll gradually build your weekly volume up to 40km and a 15km long run — all at an easy aerobic effort. Alongside the running, you’ll complete three weekly strength sessions (starting at 10 minutes and building to 30 minutes) and extended foam rolling/recovery work to help your body adapt safely.

Beginner runners are aiming to build fitness and confidence, setting themselves up for longer or more specific training later in the year.

⚡ Intermediate Plan Designed for runners with a few months of consistent training, this plan suits those currently running 30km+ per week across 4–5 sessions, with a 10km long run. Over 12 weeks you’ll steadily progress to a 60km week and a 22km long run, giving you a strong aerobic foundation without overloading intensity. Strength work is an important focus: three weekly sessions progress from 10 to 30 minutes across the plan, complemented by extended recovery routines. You’ll also complete three MAF tests (weeks 2, 5 and 9) to measure your aerobic progress.

Intermediate runners are aiming to finish the plan with solid endurance and a strong platform for race-specific training.

🔥 Advanced Plan This plan is best for experienced runners already logging 45km+ per week. You’ll start with a 44km week and a 12km long run, and progress to a 74km week and long run of 27km. Training remains almost entirely in Zone 2 to maximise aerobic development while avoiding burnout. A strong emphasis on conditioning supports the mileage: three weekly strength sessions gradually increase in duration, while longer foam rolling and massage ball work ensure you recover well. MAF tests are built in to help track improvements in aerobic efficiency.

Advanced runners are aiming to build exceptional aerobic strength and durability, ready to transition into higher-intensity or race-specific training with confidence.

This chart shows the long run distance and total weekly volume for each of the three levels. It can help you to choose which level of the plan is the most appropriate one to follow. It will also help you plan your long runs in advance.

Choose the level that suits your current level of fitness. e.g. if you have consistently been running 20 – 25km per week for the past few months then choose the beginner level. The intermediate and advanced plans will be too much of a step up. You can always change levels during the plan if you are finding it too easy or too hard.

Session Descriptions (in alphabetical order)

Accelerations are 20 to 40 second efforts building from an easy jog to a relaxed hard effort, and then easing back down to a jog again. Focus on running tall and keeping your cadence high and your strides short. Slowly walk or jog for 1 minute between accelerations. The purpose of accelerations is to improve your leg speed and your stride mechanics. Keep in mind that they are meant to be fun, and something to look forward to after an easy run. They are NOT a sprinting session.

You should be able to talk comfortably in normal sentences when running at an aerobic pace. The purpose of these sessions is to add more mileage to your week without causing too much fatigue. Aerobic runs improve your running economy to make you a more efficient runner. Use the 180 Formula covered in your training plan and calculate your Maximum Aerobic Training Heart Rate (MATHR) to work out a more precise measure of your aerobic pace.

Cross training could be swimming, or cycling, or pilates or yoga or a low impact gym class. NB: 30mins for aerobic activities like swimming, cycling and gym. 60 mins for Pilates or Yoga or Stretching Class. These sessions are good for your body as they use different muscle groups and are low impact. Don’t perform these sessions if you are feeling too fatigued from the current training load

These elevation profiles are a measure of the total amount of vertical elevation during a run. Your total elevation can be measured by most current GPS watches, or you can run with your phone and download an app called Strava which will record your elevation. NB: The ELEV figures in this program are guidelines, they do not have to be adhered to exactly.

Pick a flat course for these runs. A few small undulations is ok if you don’t have access to completely flat ground.The purpose of these flat runs is active recovery. They are to help increase your mileage safely, without causing too much fatigue to your system.

I suggest you make as many of your long runs as possible on trail. Trail running is more forgiving on your body due to the variation in your stride pattern caused by the changing terrain. You are also training for a trail event, so training on trails is more race-specific.
A MAF test is a way to objectively measure your current level of aerobic fitness.

Pick your running route carefully for the weekend trail run. Ideally you want to pick something with similar terrain to your goal event. It takes practice and experience to run efficiently on trails, so the sooner you start training on them the better.

During the recovery weeks there is less total volume and less total elevation. We continue with some easy accelerations during the recovery week to help maintain your leg speed and running confidence. There is also the option of swapping the Sunday long run for a trail hike instead. This will allow more time on your feet, but with a low heart rate and less impact. The purpose of a recovery week is to let your body and your immune system recover. It will also help to reduce any muscle tightness and niggles. These weeks will help to restore your energy for the next training build phase. Do not run over the stated volumes or it won’t actually be a recovery week.

Rest days are vital to help your body recover from the training sessions. Without adequate rest you are more likely to become ill and injured. Try to get as much sleep and recovery time as possible on these days.

Rolling hills is the term we use to describe running over a course that is consistently going up and downhill for the duration of your run. Plan ahead and identify a course that has a good amount of up and downhill. The hills don’t have to be steep but they should be as regular as possible throughout the course. Consider running a short hilly loop multiple times if you don’t have access to a long hilly route. You should average approximately 200m – 250m of vertical elevation per hour of running on rolling hills.

THESE ARE WALKING REPEATS – NOT RUNNING. Find a set of stairs with around 50 – 100 steps if possible. You should perform these stair repeats during the middle portion of your run (after a short warm up and before a short cool down). For these stair repeats you should initially walk up 1 step at a time, but you can progress to 2 steps at a time if you can keep your heart rate low (this depends on your level of aerobic fitness). Walk slowly back down the stairs to recover. Repeat for the stated duration on the training plan.

A routine of exercises including stretching, stability, and strengthening. There will be regular changes to the exercises included in the routine, to focus on different body parts as required to compliment the training program and build your stronger more stable body.

NB: These exercises are an integral part of this training program. The Strength and Stability sessions are equally as important as the running sessions.
